description: Errors found by semantic analysis: names that are not declared, types that do not match, wrong number of arguments...

rules.title: Name used but never declared
patterns: ^'(?P<name>[^']+)' undeclared \(first use in this function\)(?:; did you mean '(?P<suggest>[^']+)'\?)?$
^'(?P<name>[^']+)' undeclared here \(not in a function\)(?:; did you mean '(?P<suggest>[^']+)'\?)?$
^'(?P<name>[^']+)' was not declared in this scope(?:; did you mean '(?P<suggest>[^']+)'\?)?$
^use of undeclared identifier '(?P<name>[^']+)'(?:; did you mean '(?P<suggest>[^']+)'\?)?$
^'(?P<name>[^']+)' is not a member of 'std'(?:; did you mean '(?P<suggest>[^']+)'\?)?$
^no member named '(?P<name>[^']+)' in namespace 'std'(?:; did you mean '(?P<suggest>[^']+)'\?)?$
rules.what: You used the name `{name}` on line {line}, but the compiler has never seen it declared (created) before this line.
why: A spelling mistake - C/C++ is case-sensitive, so `Count` and `count` are different names.
The variable was declared inside another block `{ }` (or a for loop) and does not exist here.
The variable is declared later in the code, after this line.
A library name is used without its `#include`.
fix: Declare `{name}` before using it, e.g. `int {name} = 0;`, or fix the spelling.
samples: 'conut' undeclared (first use in this function); did you mean 'count'?
use of undeclared identifier 'i'
'cout' was not declared in this scope; did you mean 'std::cout'?

rules.title: Function called before it is declared
patterns: ^implicit declaration of function '(?P<name>[^']+)'(?:; did you mean '(?P<suggest>[^']+)'\?)?$
^call to undeclared (?:library )?function '(?P<name>[^']+)'(?: with type '(?P<type>.+?)')?; ISO C99 and later do not support implicit function declarations$
rules.what: The function `{name}` is called on line {line}, but the compiler has not seen any declaration of it yet.
why: The `#include` for a library function is missing (printf needs stdio.h, strlen needs string.h, sqrt needs math.h ...).
Your own function is written AFTER main() and has no prototype above main().
The function name is misspelled.
fix: Add the right `#include`, or put a prototype of `{name}` above main().
rules.tip: Since C99 calling an undeclared function is an error (Clang and GCC 14+ refuse to compile it). Older GCC only warns and guesses that it returns int - which often causes wrong results.
samples: implicit declaration of function 'printf'
call to undeclared library function 'strcpy' with type 'char *(char *, const char *)'; ISO C99 and later do not support implicit function declarations
implicit declaration of function 'prinft'; did you mean 'printf'?

rules.title: Missing return type (implicit int)
patterns: ^ISO C\+\+ forbids declaration of '(?P<name>[^']+)' with no type$
^a type specifier is required for all declarations$
rules.what: A function or variable on line {line} has no type written in front of it. Old C assumed `int`; modern C/C++ requires the type.
why: Writing `main()` instead of `int main()` (seen in old textbooks).
fix: Write the type explicitly: `int main()`.
samples: return type defaults to 'int'
type specifier missing, defaults to 'int'; ISO C99 and later do not support implicit int
a type specifier is required for all declarations

rules.title: Unknown type name
patterns: ^'(?P<name>[^']+)' does not name a type(?:; did you mean '(?P<suggest>[^']+)'\?)?$
rules.what: `{name}` is used as a type on line {line}, but no type with that name exists.
why: A spelling or capitalisation mistake (`Int`, `Float`, `integer`).
A type that needs a header or `std::` (`string`, `vector`, `bool` in C).
A struct used without the word `struct` in C.
fix: Use a valid type such as `int`, `float`, `double`, `char`.
samples: unknown type name 'Int'; did you mean 'int'?
'strng' does not name a type
no template named 'vector'

rules.title: Wrong number of arguments in a function call
patterns: ^too (?P<amount>few|many) arguments to function call, expected (?:at least |at most )?(?P<expected>\d+), have (?P<have>\d+)$
^too (?P<amount>few|many) arguments to function call, (?:at least argument|single argument) '(?P<param>[^']+)' (?:must be specified|was not specified)$
rules.what: The call on line {line} passes {have} argument(s), but `{func}` is defined to take {expected}.
why: An argument is missing or there is one too many.
The function was changed but this call was not updated.
fix: Call it with exactly the parameters listed in its definition: `{signature}`.

example.wrong:
int add(int a, int b);
add(5);
example.right:
int add(int a, int b);
add(5, 3);

samples: too few arguments to function 'add'
too many arguments to function call, expected 2, have 3

rules.title: Assigning to something that is not a variable (lvalue required)
patterns: ^lvalue required as left operand of assignment$
^cannot take the address of an rvalue of type '(?P<type>[^']+)'$
rules.what: The left side of `=` on line {line} is not a variable, so nothing can be stored into it. Only variables (lvalues) can be assigned.
why: `=` was used instead of `==` in a comparison, e.g. `if (x % 2 = 0)`.
The two sides are swapped: `5 = x` instead of `x = 5`.
An expression on the left: `x + 1 = y`.
fix: To COMPARE use `==`; to ASSIGN put the variable on the left: `x = 5;`.
samples: lvalue required as left operand of assignment
expression is not assignable

rules.title: Assigning to a whole array
patterns: ^incompatible types (?:in assignment|when assigning to type '(?P<to>[^']+)' from type '(?P<from>[^']+)')$
rules.what: An array cannot be assigned with `=` after it is created. You can only store values into its elements, one at a time (`a[0] = ...`).
why: Treating an array like a single variable: `int a[10];` creates 10 separate values, not one.
Writing `name = "Ram";` for `char name[20];` - this works in Python/Java but not in C.
fix: Store into one element: `a[i] = value;`.
For text in a char array, copy it with `strcpy(name, "Ram");` (needs `#include <string.h>`).
samples: assignment to expression with array type
array type 'char[20]' is not assignable

rules.title: Same name declared twice
rules.what: `{name}` is declared a second time on line {line}. In one scope each name can only be created once.
why: You wanted to CHANGE the value, but wrote the type again (`int x = 2;` instead of `x = 2;`).
Two different things were given the same name.
fix: To change the value, drop the type: `{name} = ...;`
Or give the second variable a different name.
samples: redefinition of 'x'
redeclaration of 'int x'

rules.title: Conflicting types for a function
patterns: ^functions that differ only in their return type cannot be overloaded$
rules.what: `{name}` is declared in two different ways (different return type or parameters).
why: The function was CALLED before it was declared, so C guessed `int {name}()` - and the real definition later does not match that guess.
The prototype at the top and the definition below do not match.
fix: Put a prototype that exactly matches the definition above main().

example.wrong:
int square(int x);
float square(float x) { return x * x; }
example.right:
float square(float x);
float square(float x) { return x * x; }

samples: conflicting types for 'area'; have 'float(float)'
conflicting types for 'square'

rules.title: Same name used for two different things
patterns: ^'(?P<name>[^']+)' redeclared as different kind of symbol$
^redefinition of '(?P<name>[^']+)' as different kind of symbol$
rules.what: `{name}` is used both as a function and as a variable (or similar). One name can only mean one thing in the same scope.
why: A variable was given the same name as a function.
fix: Rename the variable, e.g. `{name}Value` or `total{name}`.
samples: 'count' redeclared as different kind of symbol

rules.title: main must return int
rules.what: `main` must be declared as `int main()`, because it returns a status number to the operating system (0 = success).
why: `void main()` appears in many old textbooks and Turbo C programs, but it is not valid standard C/C++.
fix: Write `int main()` and end it with `return 0;`.
samples: return type of 'main' is not 'int'
'::main' must return 'int'

rules.title: void function returns a value
patterns: ^'return' with a value, in function returning void$
^void function '(?P<func>[^']+)' should not return a value$
^return-statement with a value, in function returning 'void'$
rules.what: The function `{func}` is declared `void` (it returns nothing), but line {line} tries to return a value.
why: The function should return a value but was declared void, or the return value is not needed.
fix: Change `void` to the right return type (e.g. `int {func}(...)`), or write just `return;`.
samples: 'return' with a value, in function returning void
void function 'show' should not return a value

rules.title: return without a value in a non-void function
patterns: ^'return' with no value, in function returning non-void$
^return-statement with no value, in function returning '(?P<type>[^']+)'$
rules.what: The function `{func}` promises to return a value, but the `return;` on line {line} returns nothing.
why: The value after `return` was forgotten.
fix: Return a value of the right type, e.g. `return 0;`, or make the function `void`.
samples: 'return' with no value, in function returning non-void

rules.title: Using the result of a void function
patterns: ^void value not ignored as it ought to be$
^initializing '(?P<to>[^']+)' with an expression of incompatible type 'void'$
rules.what: Line {line} tries to use the result of a function that returns `void` (nothing).
why: The function prints its result instead of returning it.
fix: Make the function return the value (change `void` to e.g. `int` and add `return`), or call it on its own line without `=`.
samples: void value not ignored as it ought to be
initializing 'int' with an expression of incompatible type 'void'

rules.title: Calling something that is not a function
patterns: ^called object(?: '(?P<name>[^']+)')? is not a function or function pointer$
^called object type '(?P<type>[^']+)' is not a function or function pointer$
^'(?P<name>[^']+)' cannot be used as a function$
^expression cannot be used as a function$
rules.what: Line {line} uses `( )` after something that is not a function, so the compiler tried to 'call' it.
why: Maths-style multiplication `2(x + 1)` - C needs `2 * (x + 1)`.
A variable has the same name as a function and hides it.
fix: Add the `*` operator, or rename the variable that hides the function.
samples: called object is not a function or function pointer
called object type 'int' is not a function or function pointer

rules.title: Using [ ] on something that is not an array
patterns: ^subscripted value is neither array nor pointer nor vector$
^subscripted value is not an array, pointer, or vector$
rules.what: Square brackets `[ ]` on line {line} are used on a variable that is not an array or pointer.
why: The variable was declared as a single value (`int x;`) instead of an array (`int x[10];`).
Wrong variable name used.
fix: Declare it as an array, e.g. `int {name}[10];`, or remove the `[ ]`.
samples: subscripted value is neither array nor pointer nor vector
subscripted value is not an array, pointer, or vector

rules.title: Array index is not an integer
rules.what: The index inside `[ ]` on line {line} is not a whole number (it is a float/double or a pointer).
why: The loop/index variable was declared as `float` or `double`.
fix: Declare index variables as `int`, or convert: `a[(int)i]`.
samples: array subscript is not an integer

rules.title: Operator used with the wrong types
rules.what: The operator `{op}` on line {line} cannot be used with a `{t1}` and a `{t2}`.
why: `%` (remainder) only works on whole numbers.
Structures cannot be compared or added with operators in C.
Two pointers or two strings cannot be added with `+`.
fix: Use a function or operate on the members/values instead.
samples: invalid operands to binary % (have 'double' and 'int')
invalid operands to binary expression ('double' and 'int')

rules.title: Use -> for pointers, not .
patterns: ^'(?P<name>[^']+)' is a pointer; did you mean to use '->'\?$
^request for member '(?P<member>[^']+)' in '(?P<name>[^']+)', which is of pointer type '(?P<type>[^']+)' \(maybe you meant to use '->' \?\)$
^member reference type '(?P<type>[^']+)' is a pointer; did you mean to use '->'\?$
rules.what: `{name}` is a POINTER to a structure. To reach a member through a pointer you must use `->`, not `.`.
why: `p.x` works for a structure variable; for a pointer write `p->x` (which means `(*p).x`).
fix: Replace `.` with `->` on line {line}.
samples: 'p' is a pointer; did you mean to use '->'?
member reference type 'struct Point *' is a pointer; did you mean to use '->'?

rules.title: Use . for structure variables, not ->
patterns: ^member reference type '(?P<type>[^']+)' is not a pointer(?:; did you mean to use '\.'\?)?$
^base operand of '->' is not a pointer$
rules.what: `->` is only for POINTERS to structures. This variable is a structure itself (`{type}`), so use `.`.
why: Mixing up `.` (structure variable) and `->` (pointer to structure).
fix: Replace `->` with `.` on line {line}.
samples: invalid type argument of '->' (have 'struct Point')
member reference type 'struct Point' is not a pointer; did you mean to use '.'?

rules.title: Structure has no such member
patterns: ^'(?P<type>.+?)'(?: \{aka '.+?'\})? has no member named '(?P<member>[^']+)'(?:; did you mean '(?P<suggest>[^']+)'\?)?$
^no member named '(?P<member>[^']+)' in '(?P<type>.+?)'(?:; did you mean '(?P<suggest>[^']+)'\?)?$
^request for member '(?P<member>[^']+)' in something not a structure or union$
^request for member '(?P<member>[^']+)' in '(?P<name>[^']+)', which is of non-class type '(?P<type>[^']+)'$
rules.what: `{type}` does not contain a member called `{member}`.
why: A spelling mistake in the member name.
The member was never declared inside the struct/class.
`.` was used on a variable that is not a structure at all.
fix: Use one of the members that actually exist: {members}.
samples: 'struct Student' has no member named 'agee'; did you mean 'age'?
no member named 'agee' in 'struct Student'

rules.title: Structure type not defined (incomplete type)
patterns: ^aggregate '(?P<decl>.+)' has incomplete type and cannot be defined$
rules.what: The structure type used on line {line} was never defined (or its name is misspelled), so the compiler does not know how big it is.
why: The struct name is spelled differently here than in its definition.
The `struct ... { ... };` definition is missing or comes after this line.
fix: Use exactly the same struct name as in the definition, and define the struct above its first use.

example.wrong:
struct Student { int roll; };
struct Studnet s;
example.right:
struct Student { int roll; };
struct Student s;

samples: storage size of 's' isn't known
variable has incomplete type 'struct Studnet'

rules.title: switch on a value that is not a whole number
patterns: ^statement requires expression of integer type \('(?P<type>[^']+)' invalid\)$
rules.what: `switch` only works with whole-number values (int, char, enum). It cannot switch on strings, floats or doubles.
why: Trying to switch on a string such as a command name, or on a float.
fix: Use an if / else-if chain instead, comparing strings with `strcmp(a, b) == 0`.
samples: switch quantity not an integer
statement requires expression of integer type ('char *' invalid)

rules.title: case label is not a constant
patterns: ^case label does not reduce to an integer constant$
^expression is not an integer constant expression$
^integer constant expression must have integer type, not '(?P<type>[^']+)'$
^the value of '(?P<name>[^']+)' is not usable in a constant expression$
^pointers are not permitted as case values$
rules.what: Every `case` label must be a constant known at compile time (like `1`, `'a'` or a `#define`), not a variable or a string.
why: A variable was used as a case label (`case a:`).
A string was used (`case "yes":`).
fix: Use a literal value or a `#define`/`enum` constant. To compare with variables, use if / else-if.
samples: case label does not reduce to an integer constant
expression is not an integer constant expression

rules.title: Duplicate case value
rules.what: Two `case` labels in the same switch have the same value, so the second one could never be reached.
why: Copy-paste of a case block without changing the value.
fix: Give every case a different value.
samples: duplicate case value
duplicate case value '1'

rules.title: break / continue outside a loop
patterns: ^(?P<kw>break) statement not within loop or switch$
^'(?P<kw>break)' statement not in loop or switch statement$
rules.what: `{kw}` on line {line} is not inside a loop{switch_text}. `{kw}` only works inside for/while/do{switch_text}.
why: `break` was used to leave an `if` - but `if` is not a loop.
A `;` right after `for (...)` or `while (...)` ended the loop, leaving the block below outside it.
fix: Remove the `{kw}`, or move it inside the loop.
samples: break statement not within loop or switch
'continue' statement not in loop statement

rules.title: Pointer and integer mixed up
patterns: ^(?P<what>.+?) makes (?P<kind>pointer from integer|integer from pointer) without a cast$
^incompatible (?P<kind>integer to pointer|pointer to integer) conversion (?P<what>.+?)(?:; (?:take the address with &|dereference with \*|remove &|remove \*))?$
rules.what: On line {line} a number is used where an address (pointer) is needed, or the other way round.
why: `&` is missing (scanf and pointer parameters need addresses).
Double quotes `"a"` (a string = pointer) used where a single char `'a'` was meant.
A single character `s[0]` passed where a whole string is needed.
fix: Check what the variable/function expects: an address (`&x`, array name) or a value (`x`, `*p`).
samples: initialization of 'int *' from 'int' makes pointer from integer without a cast
passing argument 1 of 'strlen' makes pointer from integer without a cast
incompatible integer to pointer conversion initializing 'int *' with an expression of type 'int'

rules.title: Incompatible pointer types
rules.what: A pointer of one type is stored into a pointer of another type on line {line} (for example the address of a float into an `int *`).
why: The pointer and the variable it points to were declared with different types.
fix: Make the pointer type match the variable: `float *p = &f;`.
samples: assignment to 'int *' from incompatible pointer type 'float *'
incompatible pointer types assigning to 'int *' from 'float *'

rules.title: Changing a const variable
patterns: ^cannot assign to variable '(?P<name>[^']+)' with const-qualified type '(?P<type>[^']+)'$
rules.what: `{name}` was declared `const` (constant), so its value cannot be changed after it is created.
why: The variable really should change - then it must not be const.
You meant to change a different variable.
fix: Remove `const` from the declaration if the value must change, or do not assign to it.
samples: assignment of read-only variable 'MAX'
cannot assign to variable 'MAX' with const-qualified type 'const int'

rules.title: Using * on something that is not a pointer
rules.what: `*` (dereference) on line {line} is applied to a `{type}`, which is not a pointer. Only pointers can be dereferenced.
why: The variable is a normal value, not a pointer.
`*` was meant as multiplication but has nothing on its left side.
fix: Remove the `*`, or declare/use a pointer (`int *p = &x;` then `*p`).
samples: invalid type argument of unary '*' (have 'int')
indirection requires pointer operand ('int' invalid)

rules.title: Array initialised with a variable size
rules.what: The array on line {line} has a VARIABLE size (like `int a[n]`). Such arrays cannot be given starting values with `= {...}`.
why: The size is a variable, so the compiler cannot check the initial values at compile time.
fix: Use a constant size (`#define N 5` then `int a[N] = {0};`), or set the values with a loop / `memset`.
samples: variable-sized object may not be initialized
variable-sized object may not be initialized except with an empty initializer

rules.title: Array size missing
patterns: ^definition of variable with array type needs an explicit size or an initializer$
rules.what: The array on line {line} has no valid size. An array needs a size in `[ ]` or a list of starting values.
why: `int a[];` without a size and without `= {...}`.
fix: Give a size: `int a[10];`, or initial values: `int a[] = {1, 2, 3};`.
samples: array size missing in 'a'
definition of variable with array type needs an explicit size or an initializer

rules.title: Too many values in an array initialiser
patterns: ^initializer-string for (?:array of '?char'?|char array|'(?P<type>[^']+)') is too long$
rules.what: More values are given than the array (or string) can hold on line {line}.
why: The array size is too small for the list of values.
A char array has no room for the hidden `\0` that ends every string.
fix: Make the array bigger, or leave the size empty so the compiler counts: `int a[] = {1, 2, 3, 4};`.
samples: excess elements in array initializer
initializer-string for array of 'char' is too long

rules.title: Initialiser that does not fit the variable
patterns: ^array initializer must be an initializer list(?: or (?:wide )?string literal)?$
^incompatible types when initializing type '(?P<to>[^']+)' using type '(?P<from>[^']+)'$
rules.what: The starting value on line {line} cannot be stored in this variable (for example a single value for a whole array).
why: An array was initialised with one value instead of a `{...}` list.
A struct was assigned to a number or vice versa.
fix: Use `{ }` for arrays: `int a[3] = {0};`, and make sure the value has the variable's type.
samples: invalid initializer
array initializer must be an initializer list

rules.title: Wrong type of argument passed to a function
patterns: ^(?:assigning to|initializing|returning) '(?P<to>.+?)' (?:with an expression of|from) incompatible type '(?P<from>.+?)'$
rules.what: A value of the wrong type is used on line {line} - the compiler cannot convert it automatically.
why: A struct, array or string is passed/assigned where a number is expected (or the reverse).
fix: Pass a value of the type that the function or variable expects.

example.wrong:
struct P p;
int x = p;
example.right:
struct P p;
int x = p.x;

samples: incompatible type for argument 1 of 'f'
passing 'struct P' to parameter of incompatible type 'int'

rules.title: Global variable initialised with a non-constant
patterns: ^initializer element is not a compile-time constant$
rules.what: Variables declared OUTSIDE functions (global variables) can only be initialised with constant values in C, not with other variables or function calls.
why: `int n = 5; int m = n * 2;` written above main().
fix: Move the declaration inside main(), or initialise it with a constant / `#define`.

example.wrong:
int n = 5;
int m = n * 2;   /* outside main */

samples: initializer element is not constant

rules.title: Variable declared right after a case label
patterns: ^a label can only be part of a statement and a declaration is not a statement$
^label followed by a declaration is a C23 extension$
^cannot jump from switch statement to this case label$
rules.what: A variable is declared directly inside a `case` without its own `{ }` block. Jumping to the next case would skip its initialisation.
why: Declaring a variable right after `case 1:`.
fix: Put braces around the code of that case: `case 1: { int y = 5; ... break; }`.
samples: jump to case label
a label can only be part of a statement and a declaration is not a statement

rules.title: for-loop variable needs C99 mode (old compiler)
patterns: ^'for' loop initial declarations are only allowed in C99 or C11 mode$
^'for' loop initial declaration used outside C99 mode$
rules.what: Your compiler is running in old C89 mode, where you cannot declare a variable inside `for ( )`.
why: Old versions of GCC (e.g. in Dev-C++ / old Code::Blocks) default to the 1989 C standard.
fix: Compile with `-std=c99` (or newer), or declare the variable before the loop: `int i; for (i = 0; ...)`.

example.right:
int i;
for (i = 0; i < n; i++)

samples: 'for' loop initial declarations are only allowed in C99 or C11 mode

rules.title: Array size is negative
patterns: ^'(?P<name>[^']+)' declared as an array with a negative size$
rules.what: The array `{name}` on line {line} is given a negative size. An array is a row of boxes, so its size must be a positive whole number (1 or more).
why: A minus sign typed by mistake, or a calculation such as `N - 10` that gives a negative number.
fix: Use a positive size, e.g. `int {name}[5];`.
samples: 'a' declared as an array with a negative size
size of array 'a' is negative

rules.title: Array size is not a whole number
rules.what: The size inside `[ ]` on line {line} is a decimal number. You cannot have half a box: the size of an array must be a whole number (`int`).
why: A decimal size like `2.5`, or a `float` / `double` variable used as the size.
fix: Use a whole number: `int b[3];`, or convert a decimal variable with `(int)`: `int b[(int)n];`.
samples: size of array has non-integer type 'double'
size of array 'b' has non-integer type

rules.title: 2D array without the column size
patterns: ^declaration of '(?P<name>[^']+)' as multidimensional array must have bounds for all dimensions except the first$
rules.what: On line {line} a 2D array is declared with empty `[ ][ ]`. Only the FIRST size (rows) may be left empty; the compiler must know the number of COLUMNS to lay the array out in memory.
why: Writing `int m[][] = ...` like a 1D array `int a[] = ...`.
fix: Give the column size: `int m[][2] = {{1, 2}, {3, 4}};` or both sizes: `int m[2][2]`.
samples: array has incomplete element type 'int[]'
array type has incomplete element type 'int[]'
declaration of 'm' as multidimensional array must have bounds for all dimensions except the first

rules.title: sizeof on an array parameter gives the pointer size
patterns: ^sizeof on array function parameter will return size of '(?P<ptr>[^']+)' instead of '(?P<arr>[^']+)'$
^'sizeof \(?(?P<name>\w+)\)?' will return the size of the pointer, not the array itself$
^'sizeof' on array function parameter '(?P<name>[^']+)' will return size of '(?P<ptr>[^']+)'$
rules.what: On line {line} `sizeof` is used on an array PARAMETER. When an array is passed to a function, only its address (a pointer) is passed, so `sizeof` gives the size of the pointer (8 bytes), not of the whole array - the element count you calculate will be wrong.
why: The `sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0])` trick only works where the array is declared (e.g. in main), not inside a function that receives it.
fix: Pass the number of elements as an extra parameter: `int sum(int a[], int n)` and call `sum(a, 5)`.

example.wrong:
int sum(int a[]) {
    int n = sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]);
example.right:
int sum(int a[], int n) {
    /* n is passed in by the caller */

samples: sizeof on array function parameter will return size of 'int *' instead of 'int[]'
'sizeof (a)' will return the size of the pointer, not the array itself

rules.title: Keyword used as a variable name
patterns: ^two or more data types in declaration specifiers$
rules.what: Line {line} has two type words in one declaration.
why: A keyword such as `int`, `float`, `char` was used as a variable name.
Two types written together, e.g. `int float x;`.
fix: Use one type and a normal name: `int count = 5;`.
samples: cannot combine with previous 'int' declaration specifier
two or more data types in declaration specifiers

rules.title: Address (array or string) converted to a number
patterns: ^cast from pointer to integer of different size$
^pointer value used where a floating-point was expected$
^pointer value used where a floating point value was expected$
rules.what: On line {line} an array or string is cast to a number. An array name stands for its ADDRESS in memory, so the cast converts the address - not the values stored in it.
why: Trying to convert text such as "123" to a number with a cast.
Using the array name where one element `a[i]` was meant.
fix: To use one element, write `a[i]`.
To turn text into a number use `atoi(s)` / `atof(s)` from <stdlib.h>.
samples: pointer cannot be cast to type 'float'
cast to smaller integer type 'int' from 'char *'
cast from pointer to integer of different size

rules.title: Using [ ] on a function
rules.what: On line {line} `[ ]` is used on something that is a FUNCTION, not an array.
why: The array was declared with `( )` instead of `[ ]`, e.g. `int a(5);`.
A function and an array have the same name.
fix: Declare arrays with square brackets: `int a[5];`.
samples: subscript of pointer to function type 'int ()'
subscripted value is pointer to function

rules.title: Text (a string) stored in a number variable
patterns: ^(?:initializing|assigning to) '(?P<to>float|double|long double)' with an expression of incompatible type '(?P<from>char \*|const char \*|char\[\d+\]|const char\[\d+\])'$
^incompatible types when (?:initializing|assigning to) type '(?P<to>float|double|long double)' (?:from|using) type '(?P<from>char \*|const char \*|char\[\d+\])'$
rules.what: On line {line} text in double quotes is stored in a `{to}` variable. Anything in `" "` is a STRING (text), not a number - even if it contains digits.
why: Quotes put around a number by mistake: `"2.5"` instead of `2.5`.
fix: Remove the quotes: `2.5`.
If the number really arrives as text, convert it with `atof(s)` from <stdlib.h>.
